name: SynapTech GripTrue Palmar Adhesion Implant
body_location: bilateral palmar and digital — subdermal lattice across palm and finger pad surfaces
description:
GripTrue is a subdermal Van der Waals adhesion lattice implanted across the palmar surface and finger pad skin of both hands. The system uses a dense array of nano-scale polymer filaments embedded just below the dermis that, when pressure is applied to a surface, align and increase contact surface area at the microscopic level — replicating the passive adhesion mechanism found in certain biological climbers. The effect is a significant increase in friction and grip security against smooth, wet, oily, or irregular surfaces without requiring increased muscular grip force. The implant does not make the hands visibly different in texture or appearance; the filament array operates beneath the skin surface and the hands look and feel normal to the touch. Adhesion is pressure-activated: light contact produces no unusual effect, but deliberate pressing contact with an object activates the filament alignment. A simple neural toggle — trained during a one-week calibration period — allows the user to disengage the system entirely when desired, such as when washing hands or during social contexts where enhanced grip would be inappropriate.

GripTrue was designed with industrial mechanics and structural climbers in mind, and those communities adopted it immediately. Mechanics working on the underside of cargo drones or inside tight engine compartments use it to maintain tool control in awkward positions covered in lubricant. Building maintenance workers who clean and repair the exterior of GLMZ's towers rely on it as a safety supplement when working at height. Rock climbers and competitive sport climbers in the city's indoor and outdoor climbing communities have made it standard equipment, though competitive governing bodies vary in whether they permit it. Beyond the obvious physical labor applications, the implant found an unexpected market among healthcare workers — nurses and surgical assistants who need to maintain instrument control with wet or gloved hands — and among parents of infants who simply appreciate never dropping anything.
installation_requirements: Outpatient clinic or certified installer; bilateral procedure takes approximately 75 minutes under local anesthetic; same-day discharge; one-week neural calibration period required post-installation
maintenance: Annual dermal integrity check to verify filament lattice remains properly subdermal; filament array is biologically inert; occasional recalibration of neural toggle if sensitivity drifts; no battery or power system

side_effects: during the calibration week, users report unexpected adhesion events — picking up objects they intended only to touch — which resolves as the neural toggle becomes automatic
mild warmth in the palms during extended high-adhesion grip sessions
rare reports of skin irritation at filament density peaks near the finger pad centers, typically resolving within the first month
some users note a subtle change in how surfaces feel — a slightly heightened tactile awareness — that most find pleasant but a minority find distracting
cultural_context: GripTrue is one of those implants that generates almost no social commentary because it is simply too useful and too invisible to attract attention. On the Shelf and in Tier 2 working communities, it is the kind of implant that gets recommended worker to worker, the way a good pair of work boots once was. Employers in high-fall-risk environments sometimes subsidize it alongside the LumbarFrame as part of a standard workplace safety package. In climbing communities, it has generated the same ongoing equipment-versus-skill debate that has surrounded gear augmentation for decades, with traditionalists insisting that unassisted climbing is a different and purer discipline. Among mechanics and trades workers, showing someone your GripTrue — casually pressing your hand flat against an oiled metal surface and holding a wrench sideways by palm contact alone — is a common bit of professional showing-off that never gets old.
known_users: rock climbers and competitive sport climbers
cargo drone handlers and logistics workers
story_hooks: A maintenance worker at one of the Spire's exterior cleaning crews survived a fall from 200 meters — her safety line failed, but her GripTrue adhesion allowed her to grab a window ledge and hold long enough to be retrieved; she is now the subject of a lawsuit from the building's corponation owners who claim she damaged the building surface and is seeking damages, a case that has become a flashpoint in worker rights advocacy.

A series of high-end corporate thefts have been committed by someone who left no tool marks and no forced entry evidence — the investigator who hires the players suspects the thief is using a modified GripTrue that has been hacked to far exceed its rated adhesion, allowing them to climb smooth glass and steel surfaces that should be inaccessible.

A counterfeit GripTrue batch is circulating in the Tier 1 grey market with filament arrays that are improperly calibrated — users are experiencing involuntary full-hand adhesion lockups that require emergency clinic visits to disengage, and someone needs to find the source before a worker gets killed.
